etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Originally nyōbō kotoba for 数々(かずかず) (kazukazu, “numerous; varied”), referring to the idea of a varied selection of food served at table.
From 御(お) (o-, beautifying prefix) + 数(かず) (kazu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Contraction of 仕(し)様(よう)がない (shiyō ga nai, literally “there is no way”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/fikafika/ → /pikapika/
First attested as ひかひか (fikafika) in the 1595 Dictionarivm Latino Lvsitanicvm, ac Iaponicvm (“Dictionary from Latin into Portuguese, and Japanese”).
Reduplication of the ひか (hika-) root of Old Japanese-derived verb 光る (hikaru, “to shine, to gleam”), which root is from Proto-Japonic *pika. See also *pikaru.
As part of the Late Middle Japanese reintroduction of /p/ as a phoneme, particularly among mimetic words and in some Sino-Japanese compounds, this word regained its original /p/ sound that had by then shifted to /ɸ/.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from English orchestra, from Latin orchēstra, from Ancient Greek ὀρχήστρα (orkhḗstra).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From English camera, ultimately from Latin camera (“chamber or bedchamber”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 三(さん) (san, “three”) + 角(かく) (kaku, “angle”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*⟨poto₂ke₂⟩ → */pətəkəi̯/ → /ɸotoke/ → /hotoke/
From Old Japanese, most likely from Proto-Koreanic *Pwutukye, hence related to modern Korean 부처 (Bucheo), Manchu ᡶᡠᠴᡳᡥᡳ (fucihi); see the Proto-Korean entry for more. The word was presumably disseminated by the Baekje people of southwestern Korea, who first introduced Buddhism to Japan. The first two syllables are ultimately from Sanskrit बुद्ध (buddhá), via Middle Chinese 佛陀 (MC bjut da) or some similar Sinitic form. Thomas Pellard speculates that the final element is an ancient Koreanic word for "king; lord".
The more traditional explanation still given in Japanese dictionaries is that the final ke element might be the Chinese-derived suffix 気(け) (ke, “spirit”), but a Koreanic explanation is more plausible.
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 佛 (MC bjut), shortened from 佛陀 (MC bjut da), itself a transliteration of Sanskrit बुद्ध (buddha).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Short form of ateji spelling 仏蘭西 (Furansu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 激 is a daiyōji replacing 戟.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Reduplication of 己(おの) (ono, “self”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 圖 /图 (du).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Orthographic borrowing from Chinese 地球 (Dìqiú), coined by Matteo Ricci.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: A 国字 (kokuji, “Japanese-coined character”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Spelling pronunciation derived from Sinitic 屏 (“wall”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 大 (dai, “big, great”) + 部分 (bubun, “part, portion”).
First attested in 1903.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Man'yōshū of 759. In turn from Middle Chinese 姊妹 (MC tsiX mwojH, literally “older sister + younger sister”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/seu/ → /ɕeu/ → /ɕoː/
From Middle Chinese 小 (MC sjewX).
The suffix sense is a clipping of 小学校 (shōgakkō, “elementary school”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/ko₁/ → /ko/
From the Old Japanese stem こ (ko-). Cognate with 子 (ko, “child”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/wo/ → /o/
From the Old Japanese stem を (wo-), modern お (o-).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From the Old Japanese stem ささ (sasa-), found in terms such as 笹 (sasa, “bamboo grass”), 囁く (sasayaku, “to whisper”), and 些か (isasaka, “a little”), all related to small or slight.
Saza appears to be a later derivation from sasa.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Derived from 据(す)わる (suwaru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 思(おも)い (omoi, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 思(おも)う (omou, “to think, to imagine”).) + 付(つ)く (tsuku, “to gain, to become; to attach to, to be connected with, to come in contact with”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Appears in the Kojiki, completed 712 CE.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Appears in the Kojiki, completed 712 CE. Currently obsolete.
Cognate with 荒い (arai, “rough, harsh”), 荒れる (areru, “to become wild, rough, unkempt, dilapidated; to be violent, crazy, wild, disordered”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Appears in the Kagerō Nikki, dated 974 CE. Currently obsolete.
Plural counterpart to 分かる (wakaru, “one thing separates from another”), implying more a sense of scatter (as of many things). Intransitive counterpart to 散つ (akatsu, “to separate or scatter multiple things”), itself the plural counterpart to 分かつ (wakatsu, “to separate one thing from another”). Compare underlying root verbs aku (明く, 開く, 空く: "to open, to spread, to empty") and waku (分く, 別く: "to split, to divide").

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 文房 (bunbō, “a study, an office”) + 具 (-gu, “instrument, tool; means; ingredient”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 方法 (MC pjang pjop).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese compound 暗記 (MC 'omH kiH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Middle Chinese 柵 (MC tsrhjaek).
Compare modern Cantonese 柵 /栅 (caak³).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨siɡarami₁⟩ → /siɡaramʲi/ → /ɕiɡarami/
The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of verb 柵む (shigaramu, “to entangle”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ki₂⟩ → */kʷɨ/ → /ki/
From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨kupe₁⟩ → */kupʲe/ → /kufe/ → /kuwe/ → /kue/
From Old Japanese.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 欲張る (yokubaru, “to be intensely greedy”).
Appears in texts from 1813.
Ultimately, likely a shift from older synonym 欲ぼり (yokubori), dating to 1519.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Unclear, with multiple theories.
* From the story of the 油鉢 (yuhatsu, “pot of oil”) in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra (大般涅槃経); see 大般涅槃経#油断大敵.
*:
* Sound change from 寛(ゆた)に (yuta ni).
* There is a lamp in Enryaku-ji (延暦寺) that has been alight since the time of Saichō (最澄), its founder, and 油断 (literally “oil + end”) refers to not letting it go out.
The term is not understood in other parts of the Sinosphere.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Literally, “deviance from normalcy.”

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Derived from verb 割る (waru, “to split, to break, to crack”), as imperfect form wara- + auxiliary verb ふ (fu, indicating repetition or ongoing state: modern verb ending う u): "to be in the act of cracking up / breaking open".

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *napa. Derived from verb 綯う (nau, “to plait or twist together into twine or line”). Possibly related to Korean 노 (no, “string, cord”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Nominalization of verb 分く (waku, “to split, to divide”), from the 連用形 (ren'yōkei, continuative stem), 分き (waki). Came to refer to the space between where two things split off from each other, and then, by extension, came to refer to the side of something.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 眾 (MC tsyuwngH).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *muy. Cognate with 実 (mi, “seed, fruit, offspring”).
Standalone form of mu below. See also the etymology of 神 (kami, kamu).
Compare Korean 몸 (mom, “body”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Bound form of mi above, only found in compounds.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Compound of 身(む) (mu, “body”, bound form of standalone mi) + くろ (kuro). The derivation of the kuro element is uncertain, but it might be an alteration or ancient form of 幹(から) (kara, “trunk, main part”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 身 (syin, “body, self”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Borrowed from Middle Chinese 鐵 (MC thet, “iron”). Compare modern Mandarin reading tiě, Hakka thiet.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 黒 (kuro, “black”) + 金 (kane, “metal”). The kane changes to gane as an instance of rendaku (連濁). Compare the black in English blacksmith.
